claims.claim: The Cardiff Giant was discovered on October 16, 1869, in Cardiff, New York
claims.quote: uncovered on October 16, 1869, by workers digging a well behind the barn of William C. "Stub" Newell, in Cardiff, New York

claims.claim: Two men hired to dig a well behind William Newell's barn found the giant
claims.quote: Newell hired Gideon Emmons and Henry Nichols, ostensibly to dig a well, and on October 16, 1869, they found the giant.

claims.claim: The figure was a ten-foot stone man
claims.quote: It was a 10-foot-tall (3.0 m), roughly 3,000 pound purported "petrified man"

claims.claim: Newell put a tent over it and charged fifty cents for fifteen minutes
claims.quote: The next day, a tent was set up on the discovery site and Newell charged each visitor fifty cents for a fifteen-minute session of viewing the giant.

claims.claim: Three to five hundred people a day came
claims.quote: The number of visitors went to about three to five hundred per day as the demand for wagons and carriages dramatically increased.

claims.claim: The giant was made by George Hull, a New York tobacconist
claims.quote: The giant was the creation of a New York tobacconist named George Hull.

claims.claim: Hull lost an argument at a Methodist revival meeting about Genesis 6:4 and giants once living on Earth
claims.quote: Hull got into an argument with Reverend Turk and his supporters at a Methodist revival meeting about Genesis 6:4, which states that there were giants who once lived on Earth. Hull, a skeptic, being the minority party, lost the argument.

claims.claim: Hull wanted to prove how easily people could be fooled
claims.quote: Hull wanted to prove how easily he could fool people with a fake giant.

claims.claim: In 1868 Hull had a gypsum block quarried at Fort Dodge, Iowa
claims.quote: In 1868, Hull, accompanied by a man named H. B. Martin, hired men to quarry out a 10-foot-4.5-inch-long (3.2 m) block of gypsum in Fort Dodge, Iowa

claims.claim: Hull told the workmen the block was for a Lincoln monument
claims.quote: telling them it was intended for a monument to Abraham Lincoln in New York

claims.claim: Sculptors in Chicago carved the giant
claims.quote: He shipped the block to Edward Burkhardt in Chicago, a German stonecutter. Burkhardt hired two sculptors named Henry Salle and Fred Mohrmann to create the giant.

claims.claim: The giant was carved in Hull's own likeness
claims.quote: The giant was designed to imitate the form of Hull himself.

claims.claim: Quilts were hung to muffle the sound of carving
claims.quote: it is reported that they took steps to cover up their work during the carving, putting up quilts to lessen the sound of carving

claims.claim: Hull learned from a geologist that hair does not petrify, so the figure has none
claims.quote: Hull consulted a geologist and learned that hairs would not be petrified, so he removed the hair and beard from the giant.

claims.claim: Sand, sulphuric acid and steel knitting needles were used to age the surface and fake pores
claims.quote: Hull first wiped the giant using a sponge soaked with sand and water. The giant's surface was beaten with steel knitting needles embedded in a board to simulate pores. The giant was also rubbed with sulphuric acid to create a deeper, vintage-like color.

claims.claim: Andrew D. White of Cornell noted there was no reason to dig a well on that spot, since a good spring already ran to house and barn
claims.quote: that there was no reason why the farmer should dig a well in the spot where the figure was found; that it was convenient neither to the house nor to the barn; that there was already a good spring and a stream of water running conveniently to both

claims.claim: Yale's O. C. Marsh called the giant "a most decided humbug" and noted it was soluble gypsum with fresh tool marks
claims.quote: Yale paleontologist Othniel C. Marsh examined the statue, pointing out that it was made of soluble gypsum, which, had it been buried in its blanket of wet earth for centuries, would not still have fresh tool marks on it (which it did), and termed it "a most decided humbug".

claims.claim: Hull confessed on December 10, 1869
claims.quote: On December 10, 1869, Hull confessed everything to the press

claims.claim: It is unresolved whether the Chicago stonecutter who took the commission knew what it was for
claims.quote: While it is not clear if Burkhardt was aware of Hull's intentions

claims.claim: The line about a sucker born every minute was said by David Hannum, not Barnum
claims.quote: David Hannum was quoted as saying, "There's a sucker born every minute" in reference to spectators paying to see Barnum's giant. Since then, the quotation has often been misattributed to Barnum himself.

claims.claim: David Hannum owned the giant
claims.quote: Hull sold his part-interest for $23,000 (equivalent to $586,000 in 2025) to a syndicate of five men headed by David Hannum.

claims.claim: Barnum made a copy of the giant
claims.quote: he hired a man to model the giant's shape covertly in wax and create a plaster copy
